quiz.problem: The Checkpoint and the Final test question are the same question. Both ask the reader to spot a test that recomputes the expected value with the code's own formula (recipe `flour * (8 / servings)` vs `parcel.kg * RATE_PER_KG`), and the distractors match too: implementation-coupled or fake the function, one assertion, horizontal slicing because it covers one case. The writing guide says no Checkpoint duplicates a Final test question.
quiz.evidence: name-the-smell options: implementation-coupled / nothing wrong / horizontal slicing because it only tests flour / tautological. spot-tautological options: fake shippingCost / more than one assertion / works out the answer the way the code does / horizontal slicing because it covers one parcel.
quiz.fix:
Keep spot-tautological in the Final test, because goal 3 needs a tautological question there. Rewrite the Checkpoint to test the rename tell that the section highlights:
```checkpoint name-the-smell
On a recipe site, the agent splits the inside of `scale(recipe, servings)` into two smaller helpers. Every recipe still scales correctly, but one test now fails: it checked that `scale` called a helper named `multiplyAmounts` exactly once. What kind of bad test is it?
- [ ] Tautological: it recomputes what `scale` returns.
  > A tautological test copies the code's formula for its expected value. This one checks how `scale` gets its answer, not the answer.
- [ ] Nothing's wrong: the test caught a real change.
  > The change was inside `scale` only. Every recipe comes out the same, so nothing a user relies on broke.
- [ ] Horizontal slicing: it was written before the code.
  > Horizontal slicing means writing all the tests before any of the code. Writing one test first is the loop working.
- [x] Implementation-coupled: it checks how, not what.
  > Right. It broke on a change nobody using `scale` can see. Check the result instead: 200 g of flour for 4 servings becomes 400 g for 8.
```
The right answer stays at d (49 chars; the longest option is c at 52).

quiz.problem: All three distractors are strawmen nobody believes: written-after tests run slower, agents can't write tests without the Skill, test-first removes the need for review. Any reader can pick the right answer by elimination, so the question doesn't test the reasoning in goal 1. The right answer also repeats the Why it matters section almost word for word.
quiz.evidence: b: "Tests written afterwards run more slowly than tests written first." c: "Agents can't write tests at all unless the Skill is loaded." d: "Writing tests first means you never need a code review."
quiz.fix:
```test why-test-first
A friend says: "I let the agent write the code, then ask it for tests at the end. Same result, fewer steps." What's the strongest reply?
- [x] "Tests written afterwards describe the code, gaps included."
  > Right. A test that fails before the code exists, then passes, is evidence. One written afterwards may just describe what's there.
- [ ] "Fine, as long as every test passes at the end."
  > Passing is the problem: tests shaped to fit the code pass by construction, like the comment-limit test that never checked the API.
- [ ] "Tests written afterwards never catch anything, so skip them."
  > Too strong. They can catch some bugs, but nobody saw them fail, so you can't tell which ones check anything.
- [ ] "Fine, if you ask it for twice as many tests."
  > More tests written the same way bend to fit the code the same way. The order matters, not the count.
```
Lengths: 60 / 49 / 62 / 46.

quiz.problem: The prompt gives the answer away. "writes 15 tests in one go, then all the code" is the definition of horizontal slicing, and the right option ("in bulk, not one at a time") just restates it, so this is recognition, not spotting. The question also misses the most useful misconception, that seeing every test go red first makes a batch acceptable.
quiz.evidence: Prompt: "the agent writes 15 tests in one go, then all the code". Right option: "It wrote them in bulk, not one at a time."
quiz.fix:
```test spot-batch
Asked to build a password-strength checker with `/tdd`, the agent creates a file of 15 tests and runs them: all 15 fail. Then it writes the whole checker, and all 15 pass. Spot the mistake.
- [ ] Nothing: every test was seen red, then green.
  > Seeing red isn't enough on its own. Fifteen tests written before any code describe imagined behaviour and lock in a structure too early.
- [ ] It should have written the checker first.
  > Code first lets the tests bend to fit the code, which is what the loop prevents.
- [x] It wrote every test before any of the code.
  > Right. That's horizontal slicing. One test, red, just enough code, green, then the next, each shaped by what the last one taught.
- [ ] Fifteen tests is too many for one feature.
  > The count isn't the problem; the order is.
```
Lengths: 48 / 41 / 44 / 42. The right answer moves from d to c, which leaves right answers across the Final test at a3 b2 c3 d2.

quiz.problem: Only option b is a believable order. Options a (seams agreed last) and c (seam agreed after a test, then refactor before code) are scrambles nobody would hold. The strongest misconception the Lesson works against, classic TDD with a refactor step after green, isn't offered as a clean option.
quiz.evidence: a: "Write every test → write all the code → refactor → agree the seams". c: "One failing test → agree the seam → refactor → just enough code".
quiz.fix:
```test sequence-loop
You give `/tdd` a new behaviour to build in your project. Which order matches the Skill?
- [ ] Agree the seam → one failing test → just enough code → refactor → next test
  > That's classic TDD. This Skill has no refactor step: tidying happens later, at review, with a fresh context.
- [ ] Agree the seam → write the code → write a test → see it pass
  > Code before the test lets the test bend to fit it, and a test you only ever see pass proves little.
- [ ] Write one failing test → agree its seam → just enough code → next test
  > No test is written at a seam you haven't agreed. The seam comes before the first red.
- [x] Agree the seam → one failing test → just enough code → next test
  > Right. Seam first, then red, then green, one slice at a time. Refactoring waits for review.
```
The right answer (64) is shorter than a (80) and c (70).
